must_remember: For an ideal gas, the coefficient of volume expansion $\gamma_v$ and the coefficient of pressure expansion $\gamma_p$ are both equal to the reciprocal of absolute temperature, i.e., $1/T$.
At standard temperature ($273.15\text{ K}$), the volume expansion coefficient of an ideal gas is approximately $1/273\text{ K}^{-1}$.
Absolute zero ($-273.15^\circ\text{C}$) is obtained by extrapolating the linear volume-temperature or pressure-temperature relationship to zero volume or pressure.
Real gases deviate from ideal behavior due to intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes, requiring the van der Waals equation for accurate modeling.
Gases possess both a coefficient of volume expansion ($\gamma_v$) and a coefficient of pressure expansion ($\gamma_p$) depending on whether pressure or volume is held constant.

glossary.meaning: The fractional change in volume per degree change in temperature at constant pressure, given by $\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P$.
The fractional change in pressure per unit rise in temperature at constant volume, given by $\frac{1}{P}\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V$.
The theoretical temperature ($-273.15^\circ\text{C}$ or $0\text{ K}$) at which the volume or pressure of an ideal gas extrapolates to zero and molecular kinetic energy vanishes.
An equation of state for real gases that incorporates finite molecular volume ($b$) and intermolecular attractive forces ($a$): $\left(P + \frac{a n^2}{V^2}\right)(V - nb) = nRT$.
The fractional decrease in volume per unit increase in pressure at constant temperature: $-\frac{1}{V}\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial P}\right)_T$.
